prompt: Version control tracks ___ to your files.
Version control shows when a change happened.
explanation: Every recorded change carries a timestamp of when it happened.

prompt: Which is a real VCS benefit?
Recovering deleted work is hard without version control.
Which are real version-control benefits?
You can see ___ changed a file.
Every Git ___ holds the full project history.
explanation: This is what makes Git "distributed" — there's no single machine that alone holds the real history.

prompt: What's distributed VCS's main advantage?
A down server blocks Git history access.
explanation: Every clone already has the full history — the server going down blocks sharing, not working.

prompt: Being ___ lets you commit offline.
Git being distributed means no shared version.
explanation: Distributed just means everyone ALSO has a full local copy — teams can still work from one shared copy too.

prompt: Complete: set your Git username globally.
Complete: set your Git email globally.
--global applies to every repo, not just one.
What does git config --global set?
Which flag makes config apply everywhere?
Skip the ___ flag to set locally.
Your name and email attach to every commit.
Complete: turn this folder into a repo.
Running git init deletes any existing files in the folder.
explanation: It only adds Git's own hidden tracking folder — your files are untouched.

prompt: Where does Git store its own tracking data?
You can run git init on a non-empty folder.
Which command starts a new empty repo?
Complete: copy a remote repo locally.
git clone skips the project's full history.
explanation: A clone brings down the entire history by default, not just a snapshot.

prompt: git clone names your remote ___ by default.
Cloning alone gives you a ready-to-commit copy.
Which command starts a brand-new project?
Version control tracks every change to your files — what changed, who changed it, and when — so you can go back.
In Git, every developer has a full copy of history locally — so commits and browsing work even offline, while everyone can still push to and pull from one shared copy too.

git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace" tells Git your name once — every commit on this machine uses it (git config --global user.email works the same way). Leave off --global to set it for just the current repo instead.
git init turns any folder into a Git repository by adding a hidden .git folder.
git clone copies an existing repository — code and full history — onto your machine, naming that source "origin" by default.
Git moves your files through three areas: edit them (Working), "git add" them (Staged), "git commit" them (Repository).
Which Git area holds an about-to-save change?
Editing a file only changes the Working Directory at first.
git add moves a change into the ___.
git commit moves a staged change into the ___.
A change must be staged before it can be committed.
Which command moves a change from Working to Staging?
Committing removes the file from the Working Directory.
explanation: The file stays in your Working Directory too — commit just saves a snapshot.

prompt: Order Git's basic save flow.
Once committed, where does a snapshot permanently live?
git add file.txt stages that one file's changes for your next commit.
Complete: stage a single file.
git add stages only the file you name.
git ___ file.txt stages one file.
Which command stages one file?
git status shows which files are staged and which still need staging.
Which command shows staged files?
git status changes any files.
explanation: It only reports state — it never modifies your files.

prompt: git ___ shows what's staged.
git status shows unstaged changes too.
git add . stages every changed file in the current folder at once.
Complete: stage every changed file.
git add . stages just one file.
explanation: The . means every changed file in this folder, not just one.

prompt: Which command stages all changes?
git add ___ stages everything.
git commit -m "message" saves your staged changes with a description attached.
Complete: commit with a message flag.
The -m flag lets you skip opening an editor.
git commit ___ adds a message inline.
Which flag attaches a message to commit?
A good commit message uses the imperative mood, like "Fix login bug", not "Fixed" or "Fixing".
Good commit messages use the ___ mood.
Which is a well-written commit message?
"Fixed the login bug" is imperative mood.
explanation: Imperative mood reads like a command: "Fix", not "Fixed" or "Fixing".

prompt: Write messages in ___ mood, like a command.
git log lists every commit, newest first, with its author, date, and message.
Which command lists your commit history?
git log shows the newest commit first.
What does git log NOT show by default?
git ___ lists your commit history.
git log --oneline compresses each commit to a single short line — easier to scan.
Complete: show history, one line each.
git log --oneline shows less detail per commit.
git log ___ shows one line per commit.
Why use git log --oneline?
git diff shows exactly which lines changed in your files since the last commit.
Which command shows unstaged changes?
git diff shows changes line by line.
git ___ shows unstaged line changes.
git diff compares your files to what?
git diff --staged shows only the changes you've already staged, not the rest.
Complete: diff only staged changes.
git diff --staged ignores unstaged changes.
git diff ___ shows only staged changes.
Which shows staged-only changes?
git restore --staged file.txt unstages a file but keeps your edits in place.
Complete: unstage a file, keep edits.
git restore --staged deletes your edits.
explanation: It only unstages — your edits stay right where they are.

prompt: git restore ___ unstages a file.
What stays after unstaging a file?
git restore file.txt throws away unstaged edits, reverting the file to its last commit.
git ___ file.txt discards unstaged edits.
git restore file.txt permanently discards edits.
git restore file.txt reverts to the last ___.
Which command discards unstaged edits?
git commit --amend replaces your last commit instead of creating a new one.
Complete: fix your most recent commit.
git commit --amend creates a brand-new commit.
explanation: It replaces the last commit rather than adding another one.

prompt: git commit ___ fixes your last commit.
What can --amend change?
explanation: --amend can update the commit message, the staged changes, or both at once.

prompt: git revert <commit> creates a brand-new commit that undoes that commit's changes, keeping the original commit in history untouched.
What does git revert do?
git revert removes the original commit from history.
explanation: It leaves the original commit in place and adds a new one that undoes it.

prompt: git ___ <commit> undoes it with a new commit.
After reverting one commit, how many new commits appear?
Once a commit is pushed and others may have pulled it, use revert instead of reset — revert adds a new commit and never rewrites history others already have.
A teammate already pulled a bad commit. Safe fix?
git reset --hard is safe on commits others already pulled.
explanation: It rewrites history, which breaks teammates' copies of the branch.

prompt: ___ is safe for shared history, not rewriting.
Why is git revert safe for pushed commits?
git reset <commit> moves your current branch back to point at that commit, as if the later commits never happened on this branch.
What does git reset move?
git reset can move your branch to an earlier commit.
git ___ <commit> rewinds the current branch to it.
After git reset, what happens to later commits?
explanation: They still exist briefly and can often be recovered via the reflog, but your branch no longer points at them.

prompt: git reset has three modes: --soft keeps your changes staged, --mixed (the default) unstages them but keeps your files, and --hard deletes the changes entirely.
Which reset mode deletes your uncommitted changes?
git reset --mixed is the default mode.
git reset ___ keeps changes staged, ready to commit.
Which mode unstages changes but keeps your files?
explanation: --soft keeps changes staged; --mixed (the default) unstages them but leaves your files as they are.

prompt: A branch is just a movable label pointing at one commit, not a copy of your files. Making a commit moves that label forward automatically.
What is a Git branch, really?
A branch copies all your project files.
explanation: It just points at a commit, so the files belong to the commit, not the branch.

prompt: A branch points at one ___.
What happens to a branch label after a commit?
git branch <name> creates a new branch label pointing at your current commit, but does not move you onto it.
Complete: create a branch called feature.
git branch feature switches you onto feature.
explanation: It only creates the label; you stay on your current branch until you switch.

prompt: git ___ <name> creates a new branch.
Where does a new branch initially point?
git switch <name> (or the older git checkout <name>) moves you onto an existing branch, updating your files to match it.
Complete: move onto the feature branch.
Switching branches updates your working files.
git ___ moves you onto an existing branch.
What is the older command for switching branches?
git switch -c <name> (or git checkout -b <name>) creates a new branch and switches onto it in one command.
Complete: create and switch to feature.
git switch -c both creates and switches in one step.
git checkout ___ works the same as switch -c.
git merge <branch> brings that branch's commits into your current branch, combining the two histories into one.
Complete: merge feature into your current branch.
git merge combines two branches into one history.
git ___ <branch> brings its commits into yours.
Which branch do you merge into?
A fast-forward merge happens when your branch has no new commits of its own — Git just moves your branch pointer forward, no merge commit needed.
When does Git do a fast-forward merge?
A fast-forward merge creates a new merge commit.
explanation: It just moves the pointer forward since there is nothing to combine.

prompt: A ___ merge just moves your pointer forward.
What does a fast-forward merge require?
explanation: If your branch has commits the other doesn't, Git can't just move the pointer — it needs a real merge commit instead.

prompt: When both branches have new commits, Git makes a three-way merge — a new commit with two parents that combines both histories.
How many parents does a three-way merge commit have?
A three-way merge happens when both branches diverged.
A merge commit has two ___.
What does a three-way merge combine?
A merge conflict happens when both branches changed the same lines. Git pauses and marks the spot with <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> for you to fix by hand.
What causes a merge conflict?
Git resolves every merge conflict automatically.
explanation: Conflicting lines need a human decision, so Git pauses and asks you to fix them.

prompt: Git marks conflicts with <<<<<<< and ___.
After fixing a conflict, what do you do next?
explanation: Staging the resolved file and committing it is what tells Git the conflict is settled.

prompt: git rebase <branch> replays your branch's commits on top of that branch instead, giving a straight line of history instead of a merge commit.
Complete: replay your commits on top of main.
Rebasing creates a merge commit like git merge does.
explanation: It replays your commits one by one for a straight line of history instead.

prompt: git ___ replays commits on top of another branch.
What kind of history does rebasing produce?
git rebase -i <commit> opens a list of your recent commits where you can squash, reorder, or reword them before anyone else sees your history.
What does git rebase -i let you do?
Interactive rebase can combine several commits into one.
git rebase ___ opens the interactive commit list.
Combining several commits into one is called what?
A remote is a saved link to another copy of your repository, usually on a server. Git names the default one origin.
What is a remote in Git?
The default remote name is origin.
Git names the default remote ___.
Where does a remote usually live?
git push sends your local commits to a remote. git pull brings the remote's new commits down and merges them into your branch.
Which command sends your commits to a remote?
git pull brings remote commits into your branch.
git ___ sends your local commits to the remote.
What does git pull do after downloading?
git fetch downloads a remote's new commits but does not touch your branch. git pull does the same download, then immediately merges it in.
What does git fetch do to your branch?
git pull automatically merges after downloading.
git ___ downloads without touching your branch.
Which is the safer, quieter option: fetch or pull?
A tracking branch remembers which remote branch it corresponds to, so plain git push and git pull know where to send and fetch commits without you naming it every time.
What does a tracking branch remember?
A tracking branch lets push/pull skip naming the remote.
A ___ branch is linked to one remote branch.
Why is a tracking branch useful?
A fork is your own copy of someone else's repository. A pull request asks the original project to review and merge changes from your fork or branch.
What is a GitHub fork?
A pull request asks to merge your changes.
A ___ is your hosted copy of a repo.
What does a pull request let a maintainer do?
Small, focused commits with honest messages are much easier for a teammate to review than one giant commit mixing several unrelated changes.
What makes a commit easy to review?
One giant commit mixing several changes is easy to review.
explanation: Reviewers have to untangle unrelated changes, which slows everything down.

prompt: Keep each commit ___ and small.
Why write an honest commit message?
Feature branches isolate each change; trunk-based development merges tiny changes into main constantly; Git Flow uses long-lived develop and release branches for scheduled releases.
Which strategy merges tiny changes into main constantly?
Git Flow uses long-lived branches for scheduled releases.
A ___ branch isolates one change at a time.
What is a feature branch used for?
A .gitignore file lists patterns for files Git should never track, like build output or secrets, so they never show up as changes to commit.
What does a .gitignore file do?
Secrets belong in .gitignore, not in a commit.
Git reads ignore patterns from ___.
What is a common thing to ignore?
git clean -n shows which untracked files would be deleted; git clean -f actually deletes them, without touching anything Git is already tracking.
What does git clean -f delete?
git clean -n previews without deleting anything.
git clean ___ previews what would be deleted.
Does git clean touch tracked files?
git log -S<text> finds commits that added or removed a specific line of text, fast, without you scrolling through the whole history by hand.
Complete: find commits mentioning TODO.
git log -S finds commits that added or removed text.
git log ___<text> searches commit changes for it.
Why use git log -S instead of scrolling?
git blame <file> shows which commit last touched each line, so you can find the context behind a change, not to point fingers.
What does git blame show per line?
git blame is meant to find context, not to accuse.
git ___ <file> shows who last touched each line.
What does git blame operate on?
git bisect helps you find the exact commit that broke something by testing the middle commit between a known-good and known-bad point, repeatedly narrowing it down.
What does git bisect find?
git bisect needs a known-good and known-bad commit.
git ___ narrows down the exact broken commit.
How does git bisect narrow the search?
explanation: Testing the midpoint between a known-good and known-bad commit halves the search space each time.

prompt: git tag <name> marks a specific commit permanently, like v2.0, so you can always find exactly what shipped in that release.
Complete: tag the current commit as v2.0.
A tag marks one specific commit permanently.
git ___ <name> marks a commit as a release.
What is a tag typically used for?
git stash sets aside your uncommitted changes so you can switch tasks with a clean working directory, then git stash pop brings them back.
What does git stash do?
git stash pop brings your stashed changes back.
git stash ___ restores your set-aside changes.
Why stash before switching branches?
explanation: Git blocks a branch switch when uncommitted changes would conflict with the branch you're moving to.

prompt: git cherry-pick <commit> copies just that one commit onto your current branch, without merging everything else from its original branch.
git ___ <commit> copies just one commit.
Cherry-picking brings the whole branch, not just one commit.
explanation: It copies only the one commit you name, nothing else from that branch.

prompt: git ___ copies just one commit onto your branch.
How many commits does cherry-pick copy?

Never rewrite commits others already pulled — it breaks their history. If you truly must, use git push --force-with-lease, which checks nobody else has pushed since you last fetched — never plain --force, which skips that check.
Which force-push option is safer?
You should rewrite commits others already pulled.
explanation: It breaks their local history, so only rewrite commits nobody else has yet.

prompt: git push --force-with-___ is the safer option.
What does --force-with-lease check first?
explanation: It checks nobody else has pushed to the branch since you last fetched, refusing to overwrite their work.

prompt: git reflog records every place your branches have pointed, even after a reset or a deleted branch, so you can usually find and recover a commit you thought was gone.
What does git reflog record?
The reflog can help recover a commit lost by reset.
git ___ shows where your branches used to point.
Why is the reflog called a safety net?
Committed to the wrong branch, forgot a file, or typed a bad commit message — these are all everyday mistakes with calm, known fixes, not disasters.
Most everyday Git mistakes have calm, known ___.
Wrong-branch commits are what kind of problem?
A bad commit message is a ___ mistake.
Forgetting a file in a commit means starting over.
explanation: You can add the file and amend the commit instead of starting over.

prompt: A submodule embeds one Git repository inside another at a fixed commit, so the parent repo tracks exactly which version of the dependency it uses.
What does a submodule track in the parent repo?
A submodule is a whole separate repository inside another.
A ___ embeds one repo inside another.
Why is a submodule trickier than a normal folder?

Git isn’t built for huge binary files — it stores a full new copy in history every time one changes, bloating the repo. Git LFS stores large files, like videos or design files, outside that normal history and swaps in a small pointer instead, keeping the repo fast.
What does Git LFS replace a large file with?
Git normally struggles with huge binary files.
Git ___ keeps large files out of normal history.
What kind of file is a good LFS candidate?
Git stores three kinds of objects: blobs hold file contents, trees hold folder structure, and commits point at a tree plus their parent commit.
In Git's object model what does a blob store?
A tree object holds folder structure.
A commit points at a tree plus its ___.
Which object stores a file's actual content?
How many commands does git switch -c use?
git init creates a hidden ___ folder.
git init doesn't just start tracking — it creates a hidden .git folder inside your project, where all of Git's own history and data live.
git init leaves your existing files ___.
git init never deletes or changes anything already in the folder — it only adds its own hidden folder, so it's safe to run even on a folder full of existing files.
The .git folder is hidden by default.
What does git init create?
git init is ___ on an existing project.
git init is the command that starts a repo.
git ___ starts a new repository.
Order how you resolve a merge conflict.
options: Edit the conflicted file|git add|git commit
